title: Why Do I Keep Getting Sick? Common Causes, When to Worry and the Blood Tests That Look for a Reason
summary: Why do I keep getting sick? See how many colds a year are normal, which signs need care, and how CBC, vitamin D, iron and blood sugar tests look for causes.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


**Getting sick often frequently has an everyday explanation: more exposure to viruses, too little sleep, stress, smoking, or allergies that look like a string of colds** \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]\[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \]\[[3](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/health-effects) \]\[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1713648/) \]. US adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]. Catching a few colds in a row, especially in a busy household or workplace, is common.


**When you keep getting sick without a clear reason, blood tests can check several measurable causes** : a low white blood cell count, low neutrophils or lymphocytes on a complete blood count (CBC) with differential, low vitamin D, iron deficiency, high blood sugar and low zinc \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \]\[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]. Some patterns, such as pneumonia that keeps coming back or infections that are hard to treat, point to a possible immune deficiency and need a clinician’s evaluation rather than a test you order yourself \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \]\[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \].


## Is getting sick often normal, and how often is too often?


**Getting two to three colds a year is average for adults** \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]. There is no official cutoff for “too many” colds, and the average hides a lot of variation. Colds spread through droplets and close contact, so the number you catch depends partly on how many people around you are sick \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]. Children often bring colds home, and parents often catch them \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \].


**The warning signs immunology specialists use focus on the type of infection, not just the count.** The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology (AAAAI) lists these signs that may point to a primary immune deficiency \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \]:


- recurrent, unusual or difficult-to-treat infections;
- recurrent pneumonia, ear infections or sinusitis;
- needing multiple courses of antibiotics, or IV antibiotics, to clear infections;
- recurrent deep abscesses of the organs or skin;
- swollen lymph glands or an enlarged spleen;
- poor growth or weight loss;
- autoimmune disease;
- a family history of primary immune deficiency.


Some antibody deficiencies first show up in adults, and in milder forms it often takes a pattern of repeated infections before anyone suspects one \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \]. Repeated infections from the same germ are one of the main symptoms of low immunoglobulin (antibody) levels \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \].


So getting sick three times in three months is more than average, but on its own it is not a diagnosis. Ordinary colds that clear up within days point toward exposure and everyday factors. Infections that are severe, unusual, slow to clear or keep returning in the lungs, ears or sinuses point toward a clinician visit.


## Signs that need prompt care


**See a healthcare provider promptly if a cold or other respiratory illness comes with any of these** \[[13](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html) \]:


- trouble breathing or fast breathing;
- signs of dehydration;
- a fever that lasts longer than 4 days;
- symptoms that last more than 10 days without getting better;
- symptoms such as fever or cough that improve, then return or get worse;
- a chronic medical condition that gets worse.


CDC notes that this list is not complete, and that any severe or concerning symptom is a reason to see a provider \[[13](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html) \]. A cold can lead to bronchitis, an ear infection, pneumonia or a sinus infection \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \].


**Make an appointment, rather than waiting, if your illnesses match the AAAAI warning signs above** : pneumonia, ear or sinus infections that keep coming back, infections that need antibiotics again and again, or infections that are unusual or hard to clear \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \].


A blood test you order yourself is not the right next step for any of these signs. They need to be assessed by a clinician first.


## Everyday reasons you keep getting sick


**Most frequent colds come from exposure and day-to-day habits, and no blood test is needed to explain them.** The common reasons are:


- **Exposure.** Respiratory viruses spread more easily in indoor and crowded spaces and in shared living spaces \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \]. Colds spread quickly in schools and daycares, and parents often catch them from their children \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \].
- **Short sleep.** Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night, and losing even a few hours can weaken the immune system’s defenses \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \]. Ongoing sleep deficiency can make it harder to fight common infections \[[3](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-deprivation/health-effects) \]. For practical steps, see[mastering high-quality sleep](https://mitohealth.com/blog/mastering-high-quality-sleep) .
- **Stress.** In a study of 394 healthy volunteers who were deliberately exposed to cold viruses, the rate of infection and of clinical colds rose step by step with the level of psychological stress \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1713648/) \]. More stress meant more infections rather than worse symptoms once infected \[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1713648/) \]. See[why chronic stress may affect your health](https://mitohealth.com/blog/why-chronic-stress-might-be-sabotaging-your-health) .
- **Smoking.** Cigarette smoke damages the lungs and weakens the defenses that help the body fight respiratory infections \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \]. Secondhand smoke is linked to colds too \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \].
- **Other health conditions and age.** Diabetes, heart disease and obesity can affect how well the body fights infections, some medicines and treatments lower the immune response, and the immune system naturally weakens with age \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \].


### Allergies or another cold?


**Allergies are easy to mistake for a cold that never ends.** Allergic rhinitis causes an itchy nose, mouth, eyes or throat, a runny nose, sneezing and watery eyes, often starting soon after contact with pollen, mold, animal dander or dust \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000813.htm) \]. It may come back in the same season each year \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000813.htm) \]. Fever and body aches are listed cold symptoms, and they are not listed for allergic rhinitis \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]\[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000813.htm) \]. If your “colds” are itchy, seasonal and come without a fever, allergy testing may explain them. See[skin prick tests vs blood tests for allergies](https://mitohealth.com/blog/skin-prick-test-vs-blood-test-for-allergies) .


### Why illnesses can come back to back


**Two colds close together are often two separate infections, not one that never cleared.** Colds usually last less than a week \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]. Symptoms start 2 or 3 days after exposure, and people are most contagious in the first 2 to 3 days \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \]. In a home or office where viruses are circulating, a new one can arrive soon after the last one ends.


A cold can also lead to a second problem such as a sinus infection, an ear infection, bronchitis or pneumonia \[[12](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000678.htm) \]. Symptoms that improve and then come back or get worse are one of CDC’s signs to see a provider \[[13](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html) \].


## When bloodwork helps


**Blood tests are most useful when you keep getting sick and the everyday reasons above do not explain it, and none of the prompt-care signs apply.** They check for measurable causes that you cannot see or feel directly: the number and type of white blood cells, and levels of vitamin D, iron, blood sugar and zinc \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]\[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \]\[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \].


Two practical points:


- **Test once you have recovered.** An active infection can change the results. Low lymphocytes are often temporary during viral and bacterial infections \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \], and ferritin, the main iron-storage test, rises with inflammation and infection, which can hide low iron \[[16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34028001/) \].
- **Look at the pattern, not one number.** A single slightly low value means more when it repeats, or when it fits your symptoms.


## Low white blood cells: the CBC with differential


**White blood cells fight infection, and a low count, called leukopenia, is one measurable reason for getting sick often.** A white blood count measures the number of white blood cells in your blood \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]. There are five types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]. Conditions that can cause a low white blood count include bone marrow damage, cancers that affect the bone marrow, autoimmune disorders such as lupus, and HIV \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]. See[what a low white blood cell count means](https://mitohealth.com/blog/low-white-blood-cell-count-what-does-it-mean) .


**A standard CBC reports only the total white blood cell count; a CBC with differential counts each type** \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]. The difference matters. Lymphocytes make up only about 20 to 40% of white blood cells, so a low lymphocyte count can go unnoticed if the total count is checked without a differential \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. For how each type is read, see[the WBC differential explained](https://mitohealth.com/blog/wbc-differential-explained-what-neutrophils-lymphocytes-and-monocytes-reveal) .


**Low neutrophils (neutropenia).** Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells, and they ingest and kill bacteria and fungi \[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \]. When they are too low, the main result is repeated infections \[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \]. A normal neutrophil count is above 1.5 × 10⁹/L. Neutropenia is graded as mild at 1.0 to 1.5, moderate at 0.5 to 1.0, and severe below 0.5 × 10⁹/L \[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \]. Causes include bone marrow disorders, autoimmune disease, some medicines including some antibiotics, and infections \[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \]. See[low neutrophils: causes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/low-neutrophils-causes) .


**Low lymphocytes (lymphocytopenia).** In adults, this means a total lymphocyte count below 1,000 per microliter (1.0 × 10⁹/L) \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. The most common causes are undernutrition, viral infections such as HIV and COVID-19, autoimmune diseases, cancers and medicines that suppress the immune system \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. Low lymphocytes usually cause no symptoms of their own, and they are often temporary when an infection or stress is the cause \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. Doctors suspect low lymphocytes in people with recurrent viral, bacterial, fungal or parasitic infections \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. See[symptoms of low lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-lymphocytes) . If your lymphocytes are high instead, see[causes of high lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/high-lymphocytes-causes) .


## Low vitamin D


**Vitamin D helps keep the immune system working normally, along with the muscles and nerves** \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \]. A[vitamin D](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/vitamin-d) blood test measures 25-hydroxy vitamin D, and labs report the result as deficient, insufficient, sufficient or optimal, or possibly toxic \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \]. Many experts recommend a level of 30 to 80 ng/mL (75 to 200 nmol/L), though ranges vary between labs \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003569.htm) \].


A low level can come from limited sun exposure or darker skin, a low intake from food, liver or kidney disease, poor absorption of nutrients, weight-loss surgery, older age and some medicines \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003569.htm) \]\[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \].


**What the trial evidence shows.** A 2021 analysis pooled 43 randomized trials with about 48,000 participants \[[19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33798465/) \]. Among those given vitamin D, 61.3% had at least one acute respiratory infection, compared with 62.3% of those given a placebo, a small but statistically significant reduction \[[19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33798465/) \]. The authors described the risk reduction as small, and they found no clear difference in effect by people’s starting vitamin D level \[[19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33798465/) \]. A blood test shows where your own level sits. See[symptoms of low vitamin D](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-vitamin-d) ,[vitamin D deficiency symptoms and solutions](https://mitohealth.com/blog/vitamin-d-deficiency-symptoms-and-solutions) and[whether vitamin deficiency can be behind chronic ear infections](https://mitohealth.com/blog/chronic-ear-infections-is-vitamin-deficiency-one-of-the-root-causes) .


## Iron deficiency


**Iron is one of the nutrients the immune system needs at every stage of its response, and reviews of the evidence report that even a marginal deficiency of such nutrients may impair immunity** \[[20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31963293/) \]. Iron deficiency also causes tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath, dizziness and pale skin \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[21](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \], which can feel like never fully recovering from the last illness.


Common causes include heavy menstrual periods, bleeding from the digestive tract, regular use of some pain relievers, endurance sports, celiac disease and other conditions that limit iron absorption, and stomach or weight-loss surgery \[[21](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \]. People who are underweight or pregnant are also at higher risk \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \].


**Ferritin is the main blood test for iron stores** , and a lower-than-normal level may mean iron deficiency anemia \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]. One clinical review uses a[ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) level below 45 ng/mL to diagnose iron deficiency in adults without inflammation, and below 100 ng/mL when inflammation is present \[[22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41252836/) \]. That second cutoff exists because ferritin rises during inflammation and infection \[[16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34028001/) \], so a test taken mid-illness can look normal when stores are low. A CBC adds[hemoglobin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hemoglobin) \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \], which shows whether low iron has progressed to anemia. See[symptoms of low ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-ferritin) ,[what your iron levels mean](https://mitohealth.com/blog/understanding-your-iron-levels-what-does-it-mean) and[the anemia test guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/anemia-test) . Mito offers a standalone[ferritin blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/ferritin) .


## High blood sugar


**Having more infections than usual is a listed symptom of diabetes, along with sores that heal slowly** \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]. Diabetes can affect how well the body fights infections \[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \], and complications of diabetes can reduce the body’s production of antibodies \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \].


The[HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hba1c) blood test shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]:


- below 5.7% is normal;
- 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes;
- 6.5% or higher is diabetes.


See[the two key blood tests for diabetes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/testing-for-diabetes-the-two-key-blood-tests-you-should-know) and[symptoms of high HbA1c](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-hba1c) . Mito offers an[HbA1c blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/hemoglobin-a1c-with-reflex-to-1-5-anhydroglucitol-1-5-ag) .


## Low zinc


**Zinc is needed for the immune system to work properly, and frequent infections are a listed symptom of zinc deficiency** \[[23](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002416.htm) \]. Low-protein and vegetarian diets tend to be low in zinc \[[23](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002416.htm) \]. Zinc deficiency is also more likely with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, alcohol use disorder, digestive conditions such as celiac disease or Crohn disease, and after weight-loss surgery \[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \]. Other signs can include hair loss, poor appetite, skin rashes, slow wound healing and tiredness \[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \].


**A[zinc](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/zinc) blood test needs careful reading.** Zinc deficiency is hard to diagnose, the blood sample needs special collection techniques, and a low albumin level, which is common in zinc deficiency, makes a blood zinc result harder to interpret \[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \]. A low result is most useful alongside a diet or medical history that fits. See[symptoms of low zinc](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-zinc) and[zinc benefits, deficiency and how to restore it](https://mitohealth.com/blog/zinc-benefits-deficiency-how-to-restore) . Mito offers a[zinc blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/zinc) .


## Immunoglobulins and HIV: tests a clinician directs


**When the pattern of infections suggests an immune deficiency, a clinician usually checks antibody levels and tests for HIV.** These tests answer a specific medical question, so they belong in a clinician’s evaluation of recurrent infections rather than a general checkup.


**Immunoglobulins.** An immunoglobulins blood test measures the antibodies IgG, IgA and IgM \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]. IgA protects the airways and the digestive system \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]. Providers often order it when someone has signs of low antibody production, such as frequent infections, especially repeated infections from the same germ \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]. Low levels may be a sign of an immune deficiency \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]. Causes include inherited disorders such as common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), conditions that lower the body’s protein such as kidney disease or malabsorption, and complications of diabetes or kidney failure \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]. A specialist evaluation for low lymphocytes can include immunoglobulin levels too \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. Mito lists an[immunoglobulins panel (IgA, IgG, IgM)](https://mitohealth.com/products/immunoglobulins-panel-iga-igg-igm) , which is most useful when a clinician evaluating your infections asks for it and reviews the result with you. An allergist or immunologist is the specialist who diagnoses primary immune deficiency \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \]. For the overlap with autoimmune conditions, see[the guide to autoimmune disease blood tests](https://mitohealth.com/blog/a-complete-guide-to-autoimmune-disease-blood-tests) .


**HIV.** HIV can cause a low white blood count, and people with HIV infection routinely have low lymphocytes \[[5](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/white-blood-count-wbc/) \]\[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]. CDC recommends that everyone between the ages of 13 and 64 get tested for HIV at least once, and that people with certain risk factors test at least once a year \[[25](https://www.cdc.gov/hiv/testing/index.html) \]. If you keep getting sick and have never been tested, ask your clinician about an HIV test.


## Which tests to ask for, and how to read the patterns


**A CBC with differential is the broadest single starting point, because it counts each type of white blood cell and includes hemoglobin** \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]. The other tests each check one specific cause.


What might be going on What points to it Tests that check it


Exposure, sleep, stress or smoking Ordinary colds that clear in under a week, a clear trigger \[[1](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html) \]\[[2](https://www.cdc.gov/respiratory-viruses/immune-health/index.html) \]\[[4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1713648/) \] None needed


Allergies rather than colds Itchy eyes or nose, seasonal pattern, no fever \[[14](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000813.htm) \] Allergy testing


Low white blood cells Repeated infections, often found incidentally \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]\[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \][CBC with differential](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/white-blood-cell-count) : total WBC,[neutrophils](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/neutrophils) ,[lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/lymphocytes) \[[6](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]


Low vitamin D Little sun, low intake, absorption problems \[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003569.htm) \] 25-hydroxy vitamin D \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) \]


Iron deficiency Tiredness, heavy periods, pale skin \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[21](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/iron-deficiency-anemia) \] Ferritin, hemoglobin on a CBC \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41252836/) \]


High blood sugar More infections than usual, slow-healing sores \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \] HbA1c \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \]


Low zinc Low-protein or vegetarian diet, gut or kidney conditions \[[23](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002416.htm) \]\[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \] Zinc, read with albumin \[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \]


Possible immune deficiency Recurrent pneumonia, ear or sinus infections, hard-to-treat infections \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \] Immunoglobulins and HIV, directed by a clinician \[[11](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/immunoglobulins-blood-test/) \]\[[25](https://www.cdc.gov/hiv/testing/index.html) \]


### What each result pattern suggests


- **A low total white count with low neutrophils** fits neutropenia, which raises the risk of repeated bacterial infections \[[17](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK507702/) \].
- **Low lymphocytes taken during or just after an illness** are often temporary, so a repeat CBC once you are well is the useful check \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \].
- **Low lymphocytes that persist when you are well** need a clinician’s follow-up, which can include an HIV test and immunoglobulin levels \[[15](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/hematology/leukopenias/lymphocytopenia) \]\[[25](https://www.cdc.gov/hiv/testing/index.html) \].
- **Low vitamin D** shows a correctable gap, though trials show only a small overall effect on respiratory infections \[[19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33798465/) \].
- **Low ferritin, with or without low hemoglobin,** points to iron deficiency, and the cause of the iron loss is worth finding \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/ferritin-blood-test/) \]\[[22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41252836/) \].
- **An HbA1c of 5.7% or higher** points to prediabetes or diabetes \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/hemoglobin-a1c-hba1c-test/) \].
- **A low zinc result with a diet or condition that fits** supports zinc deficiency \[[23](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002416.htm) \]\[[24](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/nutritional-disorders/mineral-deficiency-and-toxicity/zinc-deficiency) \].
- **All normal** makes these measurable causes less likely, which leaves exposure, sleep, stress, smoking and allergies. If the infections fit the AAAAI warning signs anyway, a clinician should still evaluate them \[[10](https://www.aaaai.org/conditions-treatments/primary-immunodeficiency-disease/primary-immunodeficiency-disease-overview) \].


### Mito tests for getting sick often

## Frequently asked questions


### Is getting sick 3 times in 3 months normal?


It can happen. US adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, so three in three months is more than average, but averages hide a lot of variation. A household with young children, a crowded workplace, short sleep, stress and smoking all raise the odds, and allergies are often mistaken for repeated colds. It is worth seeing a clinician if the illnesses include pneumonia, ear or sinus infections, need antibiotics again and again, or are unusual or hard to treat. If they are ordinary colds that clear up, blood tests such as a CBC with differential, vitamin D, ferritin and HbA1c can look for a cause.


### Why is my immune system so bad lately?


A recent run of illness often follows a change in exposure or habits rather than a lasting immune problem. Time in crowded indoor places, children at home who bring colds back from school or daycare, losing sleep and ongoing stress have all been linked to catching more respiratory infections. Less often, something measurable is involved, such as a low white blood cell count, low vitamin D, iron deficiency, high blood sugar or low zinc. A blood test taken once you have recovered can check for these.


### How often is too often to be ill?


There is no single cutoff for colds. CDC puts the adult average at two to three colds a year. The warning signs immunology specialists use focus on the type of infection more than the count: pneumonia, ear infections or sinus infections that keep coming back, infections that are unusual or hard to treat, needing several courses of antibiotics or IV antibiotics, deep abscesses, and a family history of immune deficiency. Any of these is a reason to see a clinician.


### Does getting sick a lot mean a weak immune system?


Not necessarily. Colds spread from person to person, so how many you catch depends partly on exposure, and sleep, stress and smoking play a role too. The warning signs of an immune deficiency describe a different pattern: infections that are severe, unusual, hard to treat or keep returning in the lungs, ears or sinuses. A CBC with differential checks your white blood cells, and a clinician may add immunoglobulin levels or an HIV test when the pattern suggests an immune problem.
